summary: The Maturidi school is one of the three accepted aqeedah schools within Ahl us-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah. Founded by Abu Mansur al-Maturidi of Samarkand, it combines rational theology (kalam) with traditional Sunni creed, and became the dominant aqeedah among Hanafi scholars across Central Asia, South Asia, and the Ottoman tradition.
overview:
The Maturidi school takes its name from Abu Mansur al-Maturidi (d. 333 AH / 944 CE) of Samarkand (in modern-day Uzbekistan), a Hanafi scholar who developed a systematic rational theology to defend Sunni beliefs against both Mu'tazilite rationalism and other theological challenges of his era.

The Maturidi and Ash'ari schools are often grouped together as the two rational-theology (kalam) schools within Ahl us-Sunnah, in contrast to the narration-focused (athar-based) Athari school. Indeed, their core aqeedah positions converge on almost all major issues. The differences between Maturidi and Ash'ari are fine-grained theological distinctions that rarely affect practical Islamic life — for example, their differing views on whether human acts of disobedience are 'created' by Allah in the same way as acts of obedience, and subtle differences in the framework of divine speech (kalam Allah).

The Maturidi school became the dominant aqeedah tradition among Hanafi scholars and thus spread throughout Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent, and the Ottoman Empire. Historically this means that much of what is now Turkey, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan, and Central Asia followed Maturidi aqeedah alongside Hanafi fiqh.

Key figures in the development of Maturidi thought include al-Bazdawi (d. 482 AH), who systematized the school's approach, and Najm al-Din al-Nasafi (d. 537 AH), whose creedal text (al-'Aqa'id al-Nasafiyyah) became one of the most widely taught introductory texts in Sunni theology.

Islam.wiki presents the Maturidi school as a fully accepted part of Ahl us-Sunnah. Where Maturidi, Ash'ari, and Athari positions differ, all three are presented as legitimate scholarly positions within the Sunni tradition.
disclaimer_note: Scholars within Ahl us-Sunnah have differed on certain aqeedah methodologies. The Ash'ari, Maturidi, and Athari schools all fall within the bounds of Ahl us-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah. Differences between them are matters of scholarly disagreement (ikhtilaf), not deviation from the Sunni mainstream.
